object.description: An arched wooden footbridge, painted pale green, crosses a pond so thick with lily pads that almost no open water shows. Willows and tall grasses close off the sky, so the whole square canvas is green, blue and pink, lit from above. This is the water garden Monet made at Giverny after 1893, diverting a stream to fill the pond and planting water lilies; he built the bridge in the Japanese style he knew from the prints he collected. In the summer of 1899 he painted the bridge from the same spot about twelve times, in a series he showed at Durand-Ruel's gallery in 1900, and this canvas, bought by the National Gallery in 1927, is one of them. It marks the point at which the garden became his only subject. Over the next quarter century the bridge disappeared from the pictures and the surface of the pond took over, ending in the panels of the Orangerie.
facts: One of about twelve views of the Japanese bridge painted in the summer of 1899; others are in the Musée d'Orsay, the Metropolitan Museum and Philadelphia.
Monet dug the pond in 1893 on land across the road and railway from his house, and planted it with hybrid water lilies.
Almost square, 88.3 by 93.1 cm; bought by the National Gallery, London, in 1927.
